proofs.proof_tex:
Fix an arbitrary finite list \(\mathcal H_0=\{h^1,\ldots,h^M\}\subset[-H,H]^K\).  The argument below uses only its finiteness and the bounds \(\lvert h_j^m\rvert\leq H\).

\emph{Exact grid embedding.}
Given \(n\) and \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\), reproduce its external randomization at the diffusion times \((i-1)/n\), and, on \(((i-1)/n,i/n]\), put
\[
 u_j(t)=\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
The conditional law of \(A_i\) is measurable with respect to the information at the left endpoint by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\text{-}predictability}\).  Hence (1) is an observed-filtration control and belongs to \(\mathcal U\) by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}continuous\text{-}observed\text{-}control}\) and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}continuous\text{-}control\text{-}class}\).  Conditional on the past and \(A_i=j\), its only nonzero score and clock increments are
\[
 \Delta X_j\sim\mathcal N\!\left(\frac{h_j^m}{n},\frac1n\right),
 \qquad \Delta Q_j=\frac1n.                                      \tag{2}
\]
On the other hand, Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\text{-}known\text{-}variance}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}local\text{-}scenario\text{-}scaling}\) give
\[
 \frac{Y_i}{\sqrt n}\,\bigg|\,(\mathcal F_{i-1},A_i=j)
 \sim\mathcal N\!\left(\frac{h_j^m}{n},\frac1n\right).             \tag{3}
\]
Induction on \(i\), using the same action kernel at each left endpoint, proves equality of the complete score--clock laws in (2)--(3), simultaneously for all \(m\).  Thus every finite policy is embedded exactly by a vertex control and has exactly the same scenario-risk vector.  Notice that (1) allows \(u_j=0\).

\emph{Approximation for continuous terminal losses.}
Let \(g_m:\mathbb R^K\times[0,1]^K\to[0,1]\) be continuous.  We show that the infimal prior-weighted risk for these losses over embedded \(n\)-grid policies converges to its infimum over \(\mathcal U\).  First, bounded progressively measurable simplex-valued processes can be approximated in \(dt\,d\mathbb P_0\)-measure by simple predictable processes \(u^{(r)}\); projecting a coordinatewise simple approximation onto the closed simplex preserves this convergence.  Consequently,
\[
 \mathbb E_0\int_0^1\sum_j\lvert u_j^{(r)}(t)-u_j(t)\rvert\,dt\longrightarrow0. \tag{4}
\]
Since \((\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\leq\lvert a-b\rvert\) for \(a,b\geq0\), the isometry for stochastic integrals and (4) imply
\[
 \mathbb E_0\left\lvert\int_0^1
   \{\sqrt{u_j^{(r)}(t)}-\sqrt{u_j(t)}\}\,dW_j(t)\right\rvert^2
 \leq \mathbb E_0\int_0^1\lvert u_j^{(r)}-u_j\rvert\,dt\longrightarrow0.    \tag{5}
\]
The clocks converge in \(L^1\), and their scenario drifts do also because
\[
 \mathbb E_0\left\lvert\int_0^1h_j^m(u_j^{(r)}-u_j)\,dt\right\rvert
 \leq H\mathbb E_0\int_0^1\lvert u_j^{(r)}-u_j\rvert\,dt.                   \tag{6}
\]

It remains to approximate a fixed simple predictable control.  Approximate each of its finitely many decision variables in probability by a function of finitely many earlier rational-time score--clock observations and the external randomizer; this follows directly by approximating bounded variables measurable with respect to the filtration generated by those observations by cylinder-simple variables.  Refine a grid so that it contains these observation times.  On every fine cell, independently conditional on its left-endpoint history, choose vertex \(e_j\) with the simplex probabilities prescribed by the simple control.  If a coarse cell contains \(d\) fine cells, the conditional variance of the discrepancy between each realized allocation fraction and its prescribed fraction is at most \(1/d\).  Hence the clock discrepancy tends to zero in probability.  Conditional on the realized clock increment \(\Delta q\), the score increment has characteristic function
\[
 \exp\!\left\{
   \mathrm i\sum_jz_jh_j^m\Delta q_j
   -\frac12\sum_jz_j^2\Delta q_j
 \right\}.                                                       \tag{7}
\]
The clock convergence and (7), iterated over the finitely many coarse cells, give a sequence \(\pi_n[u]\in\Pi_n\) such that
\[
 (X_n,Q_n)\ \Longrightarrow\ (X^u(1),Q^u(1))
 \quad\text{under the zero-drift reference law}.                 \tag{8}
\]
The cylinder approximation can be chosen on sets whose probabilities tend to one; a union bound over the finitely many decision times therefore leaves (8) unchanged.  Equations (4)--(6) and a diagonal choice extend (8) from simple controls to every \(u\in\mathcal U\).  This construction permits every prescribed simplex coordinate, and hence every realized allocation clock, to be zero.

We now transfer (8) to each scenario without asserting independence of an adaptive clock.  Under the zero-drift law define
\[
 M_m(t)=\sum_jh_j^m\int_0^t\sqrt{u_j(s)}\,dW_j(s),
 \qquad A_m(t)=\langle M_m\rangle_t
 =\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t).                                         \tag{9}
\]
Since \(\sum_jQ_j(1)=1\) and \(\lvert h_j^m\rvert\leq H\),
\[
 0\leq A_m(1)\leq H^2.                                          \tag{10}
\]
The Gaussian conditional-density calculation, applied successively to simple predictable integrands and then by the \(L^2\) approximation in (5), gives the scenario likelihood ratio
\[
 Z_m(X(1),Q(1))=\exp\{M_m(1)-A_m(1)/2\}.                          \tag{11}
\]
Its square has the pathwise factorization
\[
 Z_m^2=\underbrace{\exp\{2M_m(1)-2A_m(1)\}}_{\mathcal E(2M_m)_1}
       \exp\{A_m(1)\}.                                          \tag{12}
\]
For a simple predictable integrand, repeated conditional Gaussian integration gives \(\mathbb E_0\mathcal E(2M_m)_1=1\).  For a general integrand, use simple predictable approximants.  Their doubled quadratic energies are at most \(4H^2\), so Novikov's criterion applies uniformly and the stochastic exponentials are uniformly integrable.  Passage to the limit therefore preserves mean one.  Combining this conclusion with (10)--(12) yields the corrected adaptive-clock bound
\[
 \mathbb E_0[Z_m^2]
 \leq e^{H^2}\mathbb E_0\mathcal E(2M_m)_1=e^{H^2}.              \tag{13}
\]
Exactly the same factorization holds for every grid policy, since its bracket is \(\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_{j,n}\leq H^2\).  Thus the likelihood ratios on both sides of (8) are uniformly integrable.  Continuity of
\[
 Z_m(x,q)=\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mx_j-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2q_j\right\} \tag{14}
\]
and truncation at a level tending to infinity now imply
\[
 \mathbb E_m^{\pi_n[u]}g_m(X_n,Q_n)
 =\mathbb E_0^{\pi_n[u]}[Z_mg_m]
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbb E_0^u[Z_mg_m]
 =\mathbb E_m^ug_m(X(1),Q(1)).                                   \tag{15}
\]
Finiteness of \(M\) makes (15) simultaneous in \(m\).

Let \(G_n(\lambda)\) and \(G(\lambda)\) be the corresponding finite and diffusion Bayes values for the losses \(g_m\).  Exact embedding gives \(G(\lambda)\leq G_n(\lambda)\).  Conversely, choose a diffusion control within an arbitrary positive tolerance of \(G(\lambda)\) and apply (15).  Hence
\[
 G_n(\lambda)\longrightarrow G(\lambda).                        \tag{16}
\]
For fixed \(\delta>0\), the two envelope terminal losses of Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}terminal\text{-}envelopes}\) are bounded and continuous: exponentiation, a finite arithmetic mean, a finite minimum, and \(f_\delta^\pm\) are continuous.  Equation (16) therefore gives
\[
 B_{n,\delta}^{\pm}(\lambda)\longrightarrow B_\delta^{\pm}(\lambda). \tag{17}
\]
Every scenario loss is in \([0,1]\), so each of the four values in (17) is \(1\)-Lipschitz in \(\lambda\) for the \(\ell_1\)-norm.  Applying pointwise convergence on a finite \(\ell_1\)-net of the compact simplex and then the two Lipschitz bounds upgrades (17) to
\[
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \lvert B_{n,\delta}^{\pm}(\lambda)-B_\delta^{\pm}(\lambda)\rvert
 \longrightarrow0.                                               \tag{18}
\]

\emph{Removal of the envelopes.}
Pointwise,
\[
 f_\delta^-(a)\leq\mathbf 1\{a<0\}\leq f_\delta^+(a).          \tag{19}
\]
Taking prior risks and infima, then invoking the already established Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\text{-}terminal\text{-}comparison}\), gives, uniformly in \(n\) and \(\lambda\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 B_{n,\delta}^-&\leq B_n\leq B_{n,\delta}^+,
 &B_{n,\delta}^+-B_{n,\delta}^-&\leq\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta),\\
 B_\delta^-&\leq B\leq B_\delta^+,
 &B_\delta^+-B_\delta^-&\leq\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta).
 \end{aligned}                                                     \tag{20}
\]
Combining (18)--(20) and setting \(\eta=\sqrt\delta\) yields
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \lvert B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)\rvert
 \leq\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta).                            \tag{21}
\]
The last assertion of the quantitative comparison lemma lets \(\delta\downarrow0\), proving
\[
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\lvert B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)\rvert\longrightarrow0. \tag{22}
\]
At the point-mass prior \(e_m\), the definitions give \(B_n(e_m)=c_{n,m}\) and \(B(e_m)=c_m\).  Thus
\[
 \max_m\lvert c_{n,m}-c_m\rvert\longrightarrow0.                \tag{23}
\]

To transfer minimax regret, let \(C_n\) be the closure in \([0,1]^M\) of the achievable finite regret vectors.  External randomization at time zero makes \(C_n\) convex, and closure in the compact cube makes it compact.  Put \(v_n=\min_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m\) and \(D_n=C_n+\mathbb R_+^M\).  Then \(v_n\mathbf 1\in D_n\), whereas \((v_n-a)\mathbf 1\notin D_n\) for every \(a>0\).  Project \(y_k=(v_n-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) onto the closed convex set \(D_n\).  If the projection is \(d_k\), minimizing the squared distance along every line segment gives
\[
 (d_k-y_k)^\top(d-d_k)\geq0\qquad(d\in D_n).                    \tag{24}
\]
Upward closure, applied with \(d=d_k+ae_j\), makes every coordinate of \(d_k-y_k\) nonnegative.  Moreover \(\lVert d_k-y_k\rVert_2\leq\sqrt M/k\), since \(v_n\mathbf1\in D_n\).  Normalize \(d_k-y_k\) to coordinate sum one and take a convergent subsequence.  Its limit \(\lambda_n^\star\in\Delta_M\) satisfies, by (24),
\[
 {\lambda_n^\star}^{\!\top}r\geq v_n\qquad(r\in C_n).          \tag{25}
\]
Since \(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\) for every \(\lambda\in\Delta_M\), (25) proves
\[
 V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \left\{B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}\right\}.          \tag{26}
\]
The identical finite-dimensional projection argument for the closure of diffusion regret vectors gives
\[
 V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \left\{B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m\right\}.                 \tag{27}
\]
Equations (22), (23), (26), and (27) imply
\[
 \lvert V_n-V\rvert\leq
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\lvert B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)\rvert
 \max_m\lvert c_{n,m}-c_m\rvert\longrightarrow0.                 \tag{28}
\]

\emph{Predictable finite-policy attainment.}
Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  Choose \(N\) so large that
\[
 \lvert V_N-V\rvert+\max_m\lvert c_{N,m}-c_m\rvert<\epsilon/3,   \tag{29}
\]
and choose \(\pi_N\in\Pi_N\) with
\[
 \max_m\{L_N(\pi_N,m)-c_{N,m}\}\leq V_N+\epsilon/3.            \tag{30}
\]
Embed it by (1), obtaining a block-vertex control \(u^\epsilon\).  Equality of risk vectors, (29), and (30) show
\[
 \max_m\{L(u^\epsilon,m)-c_m\}\leq V+\epsilon,                 \tag{31}
\]
so \(u^\epsilon\) is \(\epsilon\)-optimal.

This particular control makes decisions at only \(N\) deterministic times.  Conditional on any action sequence having positive probability, its sampled Gaussian block increments have a joint density on the sampled-coordinate subspace.  For a nonempty \(I\), a terminal threshold equality is
\[
 \sum_{j\in I}\exp\{X_j(1)-Q_j(1)/2\}=20\lvert I\rvert.         \tag{32}
\]
If some coordinate in \(I\) was sampled, then, after conditioning on all other sampled Gaussian coordinates, the left side of (32) is strictly increasing in that coordinate and (32) has at most one solution; absolute continuity makes its probability zero.  If no coordinate in \(I\) was sampled, the left side is \(\lvert I\rvert\neq20\lvert I\rvert\).  The finite union over action sequences and \(I\in\mathcal I\) therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb P_m^{u^\epsilon}\{a_j(X(1),Q(1))=0
 \text{ for some }j\}=0.                                       \tag{33}
\]

For a horizon \(n\), split enrollment into \(N\) consecutive blocks with sizes differing from \(n/N\) by at most one.  Hold the action selected by the corresponding kernel of \(\pi_N\) throughout a block and feed the normalized Gaussian block aggregate to the next kernel.  The rule is predictable by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\text{-}predictability}\).  Each block clock tends to \(1/N\), and its score increment has conditional mean \(h_j^m\) times that clock and conditional variance equal to that clock.  Induction over the fixed \(N\) blocks gives terminal-state convergence to \(u^\epsilon\).  If a decision kernel is merely measurable, approximate it outside a set of probability tending to zero under the finitely many Gaussian history laws; the total probability of any altered decision tends to zero.  By (33), the probability of a shrinking neighborhood of all terminal threshold surfaces tends to zero.  Off that neighborhood the terminal loss is bounded and continuous.  Consequently the resulting \(\pi_n^\epsilon\in\Pi_n\) satisfy
\[
 L_n(\pi_n^\epsilon,m)\longrightarrow L(u^\epsilon,m)
 \qquad(1\leq m\leq M).                                        \tag{34}
\]
This proves the asserted coordinatewise risk-vector transfer.  Neither the approximation nor (32)--(34) imposes positive allocation, and no null-boundary-closure property was used.

Write \(\ell_{m,\delta}^-\) and \(\ell_{m,\delta}^+\) for the losses in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}terminal\text{-}envelopes}\).  For every \(a\in\mathbb R\),
\[
 f_\delta^-(a)\leq\mathbf1\{a<0\}\leq f_\delta^+(a).             \tag{35}
\]
Multiplication by the nonnegative weights \(w_j\mathbf1\{h_j^m>0\}\), followed by summation, gives
\[
 0\leq\ell_{m,\delta}^-\leq\ell_m\leq
 \ell_{m,\delta}^+\leq1.                                        \tag{36}
\]
If \(c_{m,\delta}^\pm\) denotes the corresponding oracle value, taking infima in (36) yields
\[
 B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq B_\delta^+(\lambda),
 \qquad
 c_{m,\delta}^-\leq c_m\leq c_{m,\delta}^+.                     \tag{37}
\]
These are bounds on observed-law design functionals and do not redefine the causal regret target \(V\).

\emph{The two continuity moduli.}
Put \(c_H=H+H^2/2\), \(s_k=x_k-q_k/2\), and \(e_I=\lvert I\rvert^{-1}\sum_{k\in I}\exp(s_k)\).  Along a line segment in \((x,q)\), either envelope composed with \(a_j=\min_{I\ni j}e_I-20\) is absolutely continuous.  Wherever its derivative is nonzero, an active intersection obeys
\[
 19<20-\delta\leq e_I\leq20+\delta<21.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \sum_{k\in I}\left\lvert\frac{\partial e_I}{\partial x_k}\right\rvert<21,
 \qquad
 \sum_{k\in I}\left\lvert\frac{\partial e_I}{\partial q_k}\right\rvert<\frac{21}{2}.
\]
Since the envelope slope is at most \(1/\delta\), integration along the segment gives the conservative bound
\[
 \lvert\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm(x,q)-\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm(x',q')\rvert
 \leq\frac{32}{\delta}\lVert(x,q)-(x',q')\rVert_\infty.          \tag{38}
\]
No division by an allocation clock is used.

For the likelihoods in the frozen core,
\[
 d\log Z_m=\sum_jh_j^m\,dx_j-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2\,dq_j,
\]
and hence, when the state displacement has sup norm at most \(d\),
\[
 \lvert\log Z_m-\log Z_m'\rvert\leq Kc_Hd.                       \tag{39}
\]
Differentiating the posterior weights gives
\[
 db_m^\lambda=b_m^\lambda\left(d\log Z_m-
 \sum_rb_r^\lambda d\log Z_r\right),
\]
so
\[
 \sum_m\lvert db_m^\lambda\rvert\leq2Kc_Hd.                     \tag{40}
\]
This remains valid when prior coordinates vanish.  Thus the normalized posterior terminal payoff \(g=\sum_mb_m^\lambda\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm\) has modulus
\[
 \Omega_\delta(d)=
 \min\!\left\{1,\left(\frac{32}{\delta}+2Kc_H\right)d\right\}.   \tag{41}
\]

Now fix a guard box and let
\[
 C_G=\max_{\text{guard box}}\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m,\qquad
 S=\frac{\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m}{C_G}.
\]
Along every segment contained in the guard box, \(0\leq S\leq1\).  Moreover, the logarithmic derivative of \(\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\) is the posterior-weighted average of the logarithmic derivatives of the \(Z_m\)'s.  Equation (39) therefore gives
\[
 \lvert S-S'\rvert\leq Kc_Hd.                                   \tag{42}
\]
Since \(0\leq g,g',S,S'\leq1\),
\[
 \lvert Sg-S'g'\rvert\leq \lvert g-g'\rvert+\lvert S-S'\rvert.
\]
Combining this inequality with (41)--(42) proves that the scaled unnormalized reference datum \(Sg\) has the corrected modulus
\[
 \widetilde\Omega_\delta(d)=
 \min\!\left\{1,\left(\frac{32}{\delta}+3Kc_H\right)d\right\}.   \tag{43}
\]
The outer minimum is essential: once the linear expression reaches one, the range bound \(0\leq Sg\leq1\) is used.

The relevant modulus propagates backward.  Couple two processes started from states at the same time by using the same future noise and feeding the second policy the first history translated by the initial state difference.  Their controls coincide and their terminal score--clock difference equals the initial difference.  Equations (38)--(43), followed by taking infima in both directions, give \(\Omega_\delta\) for the normalized posterior value and \(\widetilde\Omega_\delta\) for every scaled unnormalized continuation value.  The scaled reference-law computation below therefore uses \(\widetilde\Omega_\delta\) in every interpolation, control-continuity, mollification, Bellman-residual, finite-horizon accumulation, fixed-policy, and point-mass-oracle bound.  The coupling remains valid on zero-allocation faces.

\emph{Validated finite recursion.}
Under the zero-drift reference law, bounded predictability makes
\[
 Z_m(X(t),Q(t))=
 \exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j(t)
 -\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t)\right\}                           \tag{44}
\]
a mean-one likelihood process.  Successive Gaussian conditioning proves this for simple predictable controls.  Approximation in stochastic-integral norm proves it for general controls because the integrands have energy bounded by \(H^2\).  Thus, for bounded terminal \(R\),
\[
 \mathbb E_m^u[R]=\mathbb E_0^u[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))R].                \tag{45}
\]
The reference terminal datum is consequently \(\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm=C_GSg\).  After division by \(C_G\), its range is \([0,1]\).  At first guard exit the scaled conditional continuation therefore lies in \([0,1]\); the algorithm uses this exterior interval and makes no clamping assertion.

Suppose the vertices \(v\) of a viable state cell carry intervals enclosing a scaled continuation function \(F\), and \(y\) has multilinear barycentric weights \(\beta_v\).  If the cell diameter is \(d\), (43) gives
\[
 \left\lvert F(y)-\sum_v\beta_vF(v)\right\rvert
 \leq\sum_v\beta_v\widetilde\Omega_\delta(\lVert y-v\rVert_\infty)
 \leq\widetilde\Omega_\delta(d).                                \tag{46}
\]
Thus the barycentric interval enlarged by the corrected modulus encloses \(F(y)\).

For a time increment \(a>0\), constant allocation \(v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)\), and standard Gaussian \(z\), the reference transition is
\[
 (x,q)\longmapsto
 \bigl(x+(av)^{1/2}\mathbin\odot z,\ q+av\bigr).                 \tag{47}
\]
For each retained Gaussian cell, interval arithmetic encloses the entire image of (47).  Multiplying its nonnegative continuation interval by an outward-rounded probability interval and summing outward preserves enclosure; omitted mass is multiplied by \([0,1]\).  Coupling allocations \(v,v'\) with the same \(z\), using \((\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\leq\lvert p-q\rvert\), bounds the scaled control-net error by
\[
 \mathbb E\,\widetilde\Omega_\delta\!\left(
 a\lVert v-v'\rVert_1+\sqrt{a\lVert v-v'\rVert_1}\,\lVert z\rVert_2\right).
                                                                    \tag{48}
\]
Bounded convergence makes (48) tend uniformly to zero with the control-net radius.  Taking the minimum of lower endpoints minus this error and of upper endpoints plus this error encloses the Bellman infimum over the whole simplex.  Backward induction using (46)--(48) proves enclosure at every time level.  The identical argument, with the same corrected modulus, validates fixed-policy and point-mass-oracle recursions.  Gaussian cell probabilities have effective rational outward bounds obtained from rational Taylor bounds for \(\exp(-z^2/2)\) on bounded cells; omitted Gaussian mass is assigned adversarially in \([0,1]\).

\emph{Passage to continuous time.}
Let \(P_a^v\) denote the Gaussian operator in (47), and put
\[
 \mathcal L^v\phi=\frac12\sum_jv_j\partial_{x_jx_j}\phi+
 \sum_jv_j\partial_{q_j}\phi.                                   \tag{49}
\]
For the exact regularized recursion on a partition \(0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=1\), with \(a_l=t_{l+1}-t_l\),
\[
 J_l=\min_{v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)}P_{a_l}^vJ_{l+1},
 \qquad
 J_l\leq P_{a_l}^vJ_{l+1}\quad\text{for every }v.               \tag{50}
\]
Convolve the scaled multilinear lower interpolants on the inner score box with a rational compactly supported \(C^3\) tensor mollifier of radius \(\kappa\), whose support lies in the guard box.  Its terminal and intermediate mollification errors are bounded by \(\widetilde\Omega_\delta(\kappa)\), not by (41).  Convolution commutes with \(P_a^v\).  If the one-layer interval error, recomputed using (43), is \(\xi_l\), subtracting \(\sum_{s\geq l}\xi_s\) restores the second inequality in (50) for the smoothed lower interpolants.  Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives
\[
 P_a^v\phi-\phi-a\mathcal L^v\phi=\mathcal R_a^v(\phi).          \tag{51}
\]
Derivative intervals of the mollified interpolant and truncated Gaussian moments give outward rational bounds for \(\mathcal R_a^v\).  For fixed \(\kappa\), the score remainder is bounded by a computable multiple of \(a^{3/2}\kappa^{-3}\), the clock remainder by a computable multiple of \(a^2\kappa^{-2}\), and the interpolation contribution by the corrected \(\xi_l\).  The checked rational refinements include
\[
 \max_la_l\downarrow0,\quad
 \sum_l\xi_l\downarrow0,\quad
 \max_l\frac{\xi_l}{a_l}\downarrow0,\quad
 \kappa\downarrow0,\quad
 \max_la_l^{1/2}\kappa^{-3}\downarrow0.                          \tag{52}
\]
Because \(\widetilde\Omega_\delta(d)\to0\) as \(d\downarrow0\) for fixed \(\delta\), such refinements exist.

Linear interpolation in time then gives computable errors \(e_T\geq0\) and \(e_B(t)\geq0\) such that
\[
 \phi^-(1,\cdot)\leq
 C_G^{-1}\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm,\quad
 \phi^-\leq0\ \text{on the guard boundary},\quad
 \partial_t\phi^-+\mathcal L^v\phi^-\geq-e_B(t)                 \tag{53}
\]
for every \(v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)\), and
\[
 e_T+\int_0^1e_B(t)\,dt\longrightarrow0.                        \tag{54}
\]
For simple predictable controls stopped at guard exit, successive conditional Gaussian integrations and (51) telescope.  Since \(\mathcal L^u=\sum_ju_j\mathcal L^{e_j}\), every such control has scaled risk at least
\[
 \phi^-(0,0,0)-\int_0^1e_B(t)\,dt.                              \tag{55}
\]
All quantities are bounded on the guard box, so stochastic-integral approximation extends (55) to every progressively measurable control.  This validates the lower endpoint directly and does not invoke global generalized-terminal comparison.

For the upper endpoint, the grid recursion selects a predictable piecewise-constant policy, and the independent fixed-policy recursion, again using (43), encloses its actual risk.  Predictable simple simplex processes \(v^{(N)}\) approximate every admissible control \(u\) with
\[
 \mathbb E\int_0^1\lVert u(t)-v^{(N)}(t)\rVert_1\,dt\longrightarrow0. \tag{56}
\]
The Itô isometry and the square-root inequality give
\[
 \mathbb E\lVert Q^u(1)-Q^{v^{(N)}}(1)\rVert_1\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \sum_j\mathbb E\left\lvert
 \int_0^1(\sqrt{u_j(t)}-\sqrt{v_j^{(N)}(t)})\,dW_j(t)
 \right\rvert^2\longrightarrow0.                               \tag{57}
\]
The scenario drift difference is at most \(H\) times the first quantity.  Equations (38) and (57) yield convergence of every regularized scenario risk, uniformly over the finite scenario list.  Approximating the finitely many simple action values by the rational control net using (48) completes the upper approximation.  Combining it with (54)--(55) proves convergence of the two regularized Bellman endpoints to the same continuous-control value.  At a fixed partition, backward conditioning makes the current score, clock, and likelihood vector a sufficient Markov state.  If \(v_j=0\), (47) fixes coordinate \(j\) and (49) gives it zero coefficient; no forced exploration is required.

\emph{Guard control.}
Under scenario \(m\),
\[
 X_j(t)=h_j^mQ_j(t)+M_j(t),\qquad
 M_j(t)=\int_0^t\sqrt{u_j(s)}\,dW_j(s),\qquad0\leq Q_j(t)\leq1.
\]
Successive Gaussian conditioning and simple-process approximation show that \(\exp\{\theta M_j(t)-\theta^2Q_j(t)/2\}\) is a mean-one nonnegative martingale.  Applying Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}howard\text{-}linear\text{-}boundary}\) to both signs and using \(\lvert h_j^m\rvert\leq H\) gives, uniformly over \(m\) and \(u\),
\[
 \Pr_m^u\!\left\{\max_j\sup_{t\leq1}\lvert X_j(t)\rvert>G\right\}
 \leq2K\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(G-H)^2}{2}\right\},\qquad G>H.       \tag{58}
\]
Thus exterior intervals affect risk only through the certified probability in (58), which vanishes as \(G\to\infty\).

\emph{Minimax assembly and termination.}
Define
\[
 \mathcal G(\lambda)=B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m
 =\inf_{u\in\mathcal U}\sum_m\lambda_mr_m(u).                   \tag{59}
\]
Because \(r_m(u)\in[0,1]\),
\[
 \lvert\mathcal G(\lambda)-\mathcal G(\lambda')\rvert
 \leq\lVert\lambda-\lambda'\rVert_1.                            \tag{60}
\]
The rational simplex net with denominator \(D\) contains every point mass and has \(\ell_1\)-radius at most \(2(M-1)/D\).  The already established Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}least\text{-}favorable\text{-}saddle}\) gives
\[
 V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\mathcal G(\lambda).                \tag{61}
\]
At every prior-net point, (37) gives
\[
 B_\delta^-(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{m,\delta}^+
 \leq\mathcal G(\lambda)\leq
 B_\delta^+(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{m,\delta}^-.             \tag{62}
\]
By the already established Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\text{-}terminal\text{-}comparison}\), the width in (62) is at most
\[
 \bigl(B_\delta^+-B_\delta^-\bigr)
 \sum_m\lambda_m(c_{m,\delta}^+-c_{m,\delta}^-)
 \leq2\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta),                                 \tag{63}
\]
and \(\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta)\to0\).  Equations (60)--(63), together with the validated point-mass recursions, give certified dual bounds including the oracle offsets.

For a finite policy mixture with weights \(p_s\), suppose the independent fixed-policy recursion gives scenario-risk intervals \([L_m^-,L_m^+]\) and the point-mass recursion gives oracle intervals \([c_m^-,c_m^+]\).  Then
\[
 V\leq\max_m\{L_m^+-c_m^-\}.                                    \tag{64}
\]
This upper endpoint is valid independently of the optimization recursion that selected the mixture.

All lower endpoints converge upward to \(V\) by (43), (52), (54), (58), and (60)--(63), as the prior radius, terminal width, guard-exit probability, state and control meshes, Gaussian cells and tails, and rounding errors vanish.  Every occurrence of scaled-datum continuity in this list is charged using \(\widetilde\Omega_\delta\).  For upper endpoints, take the finite \(\epsilon\)-saddle mixture of Markov Bayes responses supplied by Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}least\text{-}favorable\text{-}saddle}\).  A net prior within radius \(r_\lambda\) of its least-favorable prior makes each component \(2r_\lambda\)-Bayes, since both a fixed policy's Bayes risk and the Bayes value are \(1\)-Lipschitz in the prior.  Equations (56)--(57) approximate the finitely many components by enumerated grid policies, which are eventually retained.  Their mixture is feasible for the rational scenario-risk linear program, while (58), (63), and the independent recursion make (64) at most \(V+\epsilon+o(1)\).  Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) proves downward convergence of the cumulative primal endpoints to \(V\).

Every candidate computation is finite.  Gaussian probabilities and elementary functions admit terminating rational Taylor enclosures on bounded cells, omitted tails use (58), and both optimization problems are finite rational linear programs.  The deterministic enumeration contains \(\delta\downarrow0\), \(\eta=\sqrt\delta\), \(G\uparrow\infty\), and the nested refinements in (52).  Recomputing every affected ledger term from (43) shows that the actual ledger sum tends to zero.  Thus, for every \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}>0\), some finite candidate has certified gap at most \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}\), so the search reaches it and terminates.  Cumulative maxima of lower endpoints and minima of independently validated upper endpoints are monotone and valid.  At termination,
\[
 \underline V_{\varepsilon}\leq V\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon},
 \qquad
 \overline V_{\varepsilon}-\underline V_{\varepsilon}
 \leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}},
\]
and the independently evaluated mixture satisfies
\(\max_mr_m(u)\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon}\).

Finally, \(\overline V_{\varepsilon}\leq V+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}\).  Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}boundary\text{-}stable\text{-}frontier}\) transfers the returned mixture's scenario-risk vector to predictable finite-horizon policies and gives \(c_{n,m}\to c_m\).  Since \(M\) is finite,
\[
 \max_mr_{n,m}(\pi_n)=\max_mr_m(u)+o(1)
 \leq\overline V_{\varepsilon}+o(1).
\]
Only the exact finite scenario list and \(\lvert h_j^m\rvert\leq H\) were used; no null-boundary closure premise is needed.  The proof establishes termination and certified convergence, but no closed-form mesh size, arithmetic complexity bound, or convergence rate.

project_justification.gap: Existing ingredients are individually narrower than the conjunction proved here. Wager--Xu and Adusumilli provide score-clock and regular-payoff diffusion architecture, and Araman--Caldentey provides a low-information posterior-control diffusion, but none proves boundary-stable transfer for the discontinuous multiple-decision loss of a fixed closed e-test. Burnett--Jennison and Ballarini et al. optimize enrichment under specified prior-weighted criteria rather than worst-case regret over a declared finite scenario list. Baas--ter Schure--van Rosmalen supplies a scalar e-value dynamic program, Rosenblum--Fang--Liu a discretized two-stage sparse program, Vovk--Wang arithmetic e-value averaging, and Howard et al. scalar time-uniform boundaries; those component techniques do not imply the robust diffusion frontier, predictable policy transfer, or the validated interval-Bellman certificate with independent recovered-policy evaluation. The complementary repository record \(\mathtt{exp\_multiarm\_secondorder\_minimax\_frontier}\) instead optimizes unrestricted design and estimation for fixed finite-population binary contrasts through an exact \(2^K\) response-type game and an \(n^{-4/3}\) second-order minimax-MSE bracket.

prose_updates.related_work: The accepted repository record \(\mathtt{exp\_multiarm\_secondorder\_minimax\_frontier}\) is complementary, not a strict-extension predecessor: it optimizes unrestricted design and estimation for fixed finite-population binary contrasts, using an exact \(2^K\) response-type game and an \(n^{-4/3}\) second-order minimax-MSE bracket with certificates. This note instead fixes the arithmetic-mean closed e-test and optimizes predictable subgroup recruitment under finite local-Gaussian scenarios for weighted missed-discovery regret, proving boundary-stable transfer at the initial state and a validated interval-Bellman policy certificate. Wager--Xu and Adusumilli supply score-clock and regular-payoff diffusion architecture; Araman--Caldentey is a low-information posterior-control donor for a regular terminal action or reward, not a source of discontinuous closed-testing transfer or minimax policy recovery. Burnett--Jennison and Ballarini et al. study prior-weighted enrichment under frequentist error control, whereas the present criterion is finite-scenario worst-case regret with an adversarial least-favorable prior. Rosenblum--Fang--Liu's discretized two-stage sparse linear program and Baas--ter Schure--van Rosmalen's scalar e-value dynamic program are complementary computational donors rather than results implying the present certificate. Vovk--Wang supplies arithmetic e-value averaging, which this note takes as fixed, and Howard et al. supplies the scalar martingale-boundary ingredient used for guard control and simultaneous inversion; neither component supplies recruitment optimization, the minimax frontier, or policy certification. The novelty claimed here is only their proved conjunction: boundary-stable transfer of the fixed discontinuous closed-e loss, robust finite-scenario recruitment, and qualitative validated policy certification.
